newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Hong Kong property developers flock to Shanghai.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Hong Kong property developers flock to Shanghai.

text.p: Hong Kong's property developers, having already created one of the most impressive skylines in Asia, are helping to re-model Shanghai at a breathless pace.
Most of the British colony's major developers have at least two or three significant building projects around Shanghai with the focus on creating top-grade office buildings.
But the Shanghai property market is facing serious over-supply with no end in sight for the building boom, leaving developers to scramble for tenants.
Property agents estimate Shanghai will have a total of 7.5 million square metres of international-grade office stock by the year 2000, equal to the entire office stock of Hong Kong.
Hong Kong developers, who have snagged many of the prime sites around the city, are trying to ride out the market downturn by targetting multi-national firms willing to pay well for the right place.
"It's location, quality and reputation," said Peter Kok, director of development and marketing for Hutchison Whampoa Ltd.

Given the glut, Hong Kong developers are becoming convinced that they will have to be patient and abandon dreams of quick Shanghai profits. Plans to build and then sell have given way to long leases and attentive building management.
"We are looking at the long term," said Charlie Lim, director of Hang Lung Development subsidiary Hang Lung China.
"If we are the owner for the next 50 years, we have to manage the building well and convince multi-nationals of the quality of the product," he added.
LIMITS ON LAND SALES, TAX INCENTIVES SOUGHT
Some Hong Kong developers have banded together and sought the ear of the local government to ask for limits on land sales and more favourable tax policies to help business along, Lim said.
Despite the risks, Hong Kong developers with deep pockets are putting significant proportions of their portfolios in China to test the waters of the potentially huge market.

They are banking on Shanghai developing into a major financial centre, like Hong Kong. Lack of a single business centre in Shanghai's urban sprawl has led them to seed projects in various locations around the city.

With costs for foreign developers of up to $2,500 per square metre to construct a quality building in the central city area, total investment for major individual projects can soar to up to $1 billion, analysts and developers said.

Over the long term, a few quality projects will conceivably earn annual returns of 12-15 percent based on rental yield over development costs in Shanghai, said Colliers Jardine general manager David Wong.
Mature markets like Hong Kong and Singapore currently yield six to nine percent returns, analysts said.
But for many of these developers, the outlook is for large numbers of empty floors, heavy discounting and fierce battles for tenants for at least the next three to five years.
"In the short term, some of the developers may be struggling," said Sam Crispin, senior manager for property agent First Pacific Davies. "The lure of Shanghai is the long term."

"Prospective tenants need to know management is going to be responsive," added Crispin. "For a lot of existing low-quality buildings, management is a cleaner pushing a mop and a bucket of dirty water."
NEW OFFICE SPACE LIMITS RENTALS

Immense amounts of new office space expected to come onto the market in the next two or three years will continue to limit returns in Shanghai, with rentals falling as low as $18 to $20 per square metre per month for some grade A buildings, analysts said.
Shanghai's premier office space now rents for between $40 and $70 per square metre a month.
"Developers are now faced with the prospect of lowering their prices substantially, and not be sure whether they can sell it or not, or to lease it," said Wong.
